strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why distributional RL can outperform expectation-based learning. Combining Sinkhorn losses with particle representations of returns is a potentially useful algorithmic direction.

Experiments compare five methods across ten Atari games and include sensitivity analyses. The learning curves show encouraging performance on SpaceInvaders and competitive results on several other games.
The manuscript cites relevant foundational work, supplies proof appendices, and explicitly acknowledges limitations concerning finite-regularization contraction and exploration under greedy policies.
weaknesses: The central probability decomposition in Eq. 4 is invalid in the stated setting. For an absolutely continuous return distribution P with mean m, P({m})=0, whereas P=(1−ε)δ_m+εμ requires μ({m})=−(1−ε)/ε for 0<ε<1. Thus the proposed remainder is a signed measure, not a probability distribution. Algebraically defining μ does not establish nonnegativity. This undermines Proposition 2 and the subsequent entropy-regularization and acceleration arguments, constituting a fundamental deficiency in the main contribution.

Theorem 1 does not establish the claimed connection to maximum-entropy RL. Its proof evaluates a newly introduced Bellman operator with modified rewards, using standard policy-evaluation convergence for fixed distributions and policy. It does not show that the original Z-fitted update implements this operator or optimizes the proposed objective J′. A cross-entropy training loss does not by itself imply cross-entropy augmentation of environmental rewards.

The stability analysis has substantially narrower scope than the claims. Lemma 1 and Theorem 2 concern a linear softmax head over fixed bounded features and apply existing supervised SGD stability results. They do not establish generalization for learned neural representations or successive Bellman-control updates. The comparison with squared loss also conflates bounded gradients with smoothness: under the same linear parameterization, squared loss is convex and smooth, with Hessian 2xxᵀ. No corresponding analysis is provided for the proposed Sinkhorn learner.

The acceleration theorem has independent proof problems. Theorem 3 specifies ε=1/(1+τ), while Appendix I uses ε=1/(1+κ); the stated choice does not produce the claimed noise bound under the given assumptions. Part (3) infers nonconvergence from an upper bound on gradient norms, which cannot establish nonconvergence. Furthermore, its point-target cross-entropy comparator does not establish an acceleration advantage over least-squares DQN.

The Sinkhorn definitions contradict Theorem 4. With the stated cost c(x,y)=−|x−y|^α, Eq. 13 gives −2 for point masses at 0 and 1, contradicting the claimed positive Wasserstein limit. Equation 12 also includes an entropy term that disappears in the subsequent definition of the transport value. Even after correcting the sign, the limiting formulas must distinguish Wasserstein powers and squared MMD; with α=2, the large-regularization limit only distinguishes means. These inconsistencies undermine the theoretical justification and leave the implemented objective unclear.

The empirical evidence does not establish the broad performance claims or adequate reproducibility. Seed counts, the interpretation of plotted uncertainty bands, a complete Atari evaluation protocol, and an implementation link are absent. Results are mixed, including substantial deficits on Qbert and Alien, and stronger cited methods such as IQN and FQF are not evaluated. There are no aggregate statistical comparisons or computational-cost measurements to assess the benefit of additional Sinkhorn iterations.

The experiments do not directly test the proposed regularization, stability, or acceleration explanations. The representation claim rests on a single Breakout t-SNE visualization, with action labels supplied by the learned policy. Projected cluster tightness does not establish improved representations or identify correct actions. Controlled comparisons, quantitative representation measurements, and evidence connecting the theoretical quantities to observed learning behavior are needed.
